```{python}
#| include: false
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.colors as mcolors
import seaborn as sns

from sklearn.model_selection import (
    train_test_split,
    StratifiedKFold,
    cross_validate,
    cross_val_predict,
    GridSearchCV,
)
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, plot_tree, export_text
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score,
    roc_auc_score,
    confusion_matrix,
    recall_score,
    precision_score,
    f1_score,
    roc_curve,
)
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance

import data2thesis as dt

navy = "#1d588c"
copper = "#b4762e"
soft = "#46586d"

plt.rcParams.update({
    "figure.autolayout": True,
    "axes.spines.top": False,
    "axes.spines.right": False,
    "font.size": 12,
    "figure.dpi": 150
})

f2 = lambda x: f"{x:.2f}"
pc = lambda x: int(round(100 * x))

# Prepare data
students = dt.load_students()
students["employment"] = students["employment"].fillna("None")
questionnaire = dt.load_questionnaire()
semesters = dt.load_semesters()

questionnaire["stress_4"] = 6 - questionnaire["stress_4"]
scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "student_id": questionnaire["student_id"],
    "stress": questionnaire[["stress_1", "stress_2", "stress_3", "stress_4", "stress_5", "stress_6"]].mean(axis=1),
    "burnout": questionnaire.filter(like="burnout_").mean(axis=1),
    "support": questionnaire.filter(like="support_").mean(axis=1),
    "satisfaction": questionnaire.filter(like="satisfaction_").mean(axis=1),
})

sem1 = semesters[semesters["semester"] == 1].drop(columns=["semester"])

dropout_data = (
    students
    .merge(scores, on="student_id")
    .merge(sem1, on="student_id")
    .drop(columns=["student_id", "supervisor_id", "workshop", "workshop_sessions"])
)

dropout_data["considering_dropout"] = (dropout_data["considering_dropout"] == "Yes").astype(int)

X = dropout_data.drop(columns=["considering_dropout"])
y = dropout_data["considering_dropout"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=2026
)

num_cols = X.select_dtypes(include=["int64", "float64"]).columns.tolist()
cat_cols = X.select_dtypes(include=["object", "category"]).columns.tolist()

dropout_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scaler", StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols)
])

tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), num_cols),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols)
])

dropout_folds = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=2026)

tiny = pd.DataFrame({
    "stress":  [1.5, 2.0, 2.2, 2.8, 3.0, 3.1, 3.4, 3.6, 3.8, 4.0, 4.2, 4.5],
    "support": [4.5, 3.0, 4.0, 2.0, 4.2, 3.8, 2.1, 4.4, 1.8, 2.5, 3.9, 1.5],
    "dropout": ["No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "No", "Yes", "No", "Yes", "Yes", "No", "Yes"]
})

tree_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", tree_recipe),
    ("model", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, min_samples_leaf=10, random_state=2026))
])
tree_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)

forest_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", tree_recipe),
    ("model", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=2026))
])
forest_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)

imp = permutation_importance(forest_pipe, X_train, y_train, n_repeats=10, random_state=2026)
imp_series = pd.Series(imp.importances_mean, index=X_train.columns).sort_values(ascending=False)

knn_grid = GridSearchCV(
    Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier())]),
    param_grid={"knn__n_neighbors": [1, 5, 11, 21, 41, 81]},
    cv=dropout_folds, scoring="roc_auc"
)
knn_grid.fit(X_train, y_train)
knn_res = knn_grid.cv_results_["mean_test_score"]

# Compare candidate models
candidate_models = {
    "logistic": Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("model", LogisticRegression(random_state=2026))]),
    "svm_linear": Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("model", SVC(kernel="linear", probability=True, random_state=2026))]),
    "forest": forest_pipe,
    "svm_rbf": Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("model", SVC(kernel="rbf", probability=True, random_state=2026))]),
    "knn": Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("model", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=41))]),
    "tree": Pipeline([("prep", tree_recipe), ("model", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=10, random_state=2026))]),
}

ranked_dict = {}
for name, pipe in candidate_models.items():
    res = cross_validate(pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=dropout_folds, scoring="roc_auc")
    ranked_dict[name] = (res["test_score"].mean(), res["test_score"].std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(10))

logistic_pipe = candidate_models["logistic"]
logistic_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
y_pred_te = logistic_pipe.predict(X_test)
y_prob_te = logistic_pipe.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

cm50 = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_te, labels=[1, 0])
tp50 = cm50[0, 0]
n_yes = int((y_test == 1).sum())

cv_predictions = cross_val_predict(
    logistic_pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=dropout_folds, method="predict_proba"
)[:, 1]

threshold_rows = []
for t in [0.5, 0.4, 0.3, 0.2, 0.15, 0.1]:
    flags = (cv_predictions >= t).astype(int)
    tn_c, fp_c, fn_c, tp_c = confusion_matrix(y_train, flags, labels=[0, 1]).ravel()
    threshold_rows.append({
        "threshold": t,
        "flagged": flags.mean(),
        "recall": tp_c / (tp_c + fn_c),
        "precision": tp_c / (tp_c + fp_c) if (tp_c + fp_c) > 0 else 0,
        "specificity": tn_c / (tn_c + fp_c)
    })
threshold_table = pd.DataFrame(threshold_rows)

cost_miss = 10
cost_false_alarm = 1
cost_rows = []
for t in np.arange(0.02, 0.62, 0.02):
    m = np.sum((cv_predictions < t) & (y_train == 1))
    fa = np.sum((cv_predictions >= t) & (y_train == 0))
    cost_rows.append({"threshold": round(t, 2), "total_cost": cost_miss * m + cost_false_alarm * fa, "flagged": np.mean(cv_predictions >= t)})
cost_curve = pd.DataFrame(cost_rows)
best_cost = cost_curve.loc[cost_curve["total_cost"].idxmin()]

flags_te_02 = (y_prob_te >= 0.2).astype(int)
cm20 = confusion_matrix(y_test, flags_te_02, labels=[1, 0])
tp20 = cm20[0, 0]
flag20 = int((flags_te_02 == 1).sum())

balanced_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", dropout_recipe),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", random_state=2026))
])
bal_cv = cross_validate(balanced_pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=dropout_folds, scoring=["roc_auc", "recall"])
up_auc = bal_cv["test_roc_auc"].mean()
up_sens = bal_cv["test_recall"].mean()
```

# Classification Models

From predicted probabilities to decisions about people

**Chapter 12**

Polla Fattah

---

## By the end of today you can

- explain how trees, random forests, k-nearest neighbours, and SVMs classify;
- fit each with scikit-learn, and compare them fairly;
- read a confusion matrix;
- calculate sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1;
- choose a threshold from the costs of the two errors;
- handle an imbalanced outcome, and say what resampling changes.

---

## Two questions about a classifier

1. Would more flexible methods rank the cases better than logistic regression?
2. What happens when predictions become decisions?

Every decision rule flags some cases wrongly and misses others. The balance depends on what each error costs, and to whom.

---

## Same data, same split, same folds

```python
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.25, stratify=y, random_state=2026
)

dropout_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", Pipeline([("imp", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scaler", StandardScaler())]), num_cols),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols)
])

dropout_folds = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=2026)
```

Exactly as in Chapter 11, so every model is trained and tested on the same students.

---

## A decision tree asks questions

```python
tiny_tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(min_samples_split=2, criterion="gini", random_state=2026)
tiny_tree.fit(tiny[["stress", "support"]], (tiny["dropout"] == "Yes").astype(int))
```

Twelve imaginary students, four considering dropout:

1. "Is support $\le$ 2.75?" puts seven, all "No", on one side.
2. "Is stress > 3.1?" separates the rest perfectly.

---

## How a tree chooses its questions

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| node | a question and the students who reached it |
| leaf | a final node, with a predicted class |
| Gini impurity | 0 when a group holds only one class |

The tree tries every predictor and cut-off, and picks the one that makes the child groups most pure.

---

## Why trees are attractive

- easy to explain;
- no dummy variables or normalisation needed;
- interactions captured automatically: stress matters only for low-support students.

```python
tree_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    ("num", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), num_cols),
    ("cat", OneHotEncoder(drop="first", sparse_output=False, handle_unknown="ignore"), cat_cols)
])
```

---

## A depth-3 tree for dropout

```{python}
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.4
feature_names = [f.split("__")[-1] for f in tree_pipe.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out()]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.4))
plot_tree(
    tree_pipe.named_steps["model"],
    feature_names=feature_names,
    class_names=["No", "Yes"],
    filled=True,
    rounded=True,
    fontsize=8,
    ax=ax
)
plt.show()
```

The top split is on `support`. Students meeting each condition branch to the left.

---

## A single tree is unstable

A slightly different sample of students can produce a completely different tree.

A deep tree overfits (Chapter 11).

The next method turns this weakness into a strength.

---

## Random forests

- grow hundreds of trees;
- each on a **bootstrap sample** of the students;
- each split chooses from a random subset of predictors (`max_features`);
- let the trees vote: $P(\text{Yes})$ is the share voting "Yes".

Each tree overfits in its own way; many errors cancel out. An **ensemble** of trees [@breiman2001].

---

## Fitting a forest

```python
forest_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", tree_recipe),
    ("model", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=2026))
])
forest_fit = forest_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train)
```

500 trees cannot be drawn: a black box. **Permutation importance** opens it a little.

---

## What the forest relies on

```{python}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.9
top_imp = imp_series.head(10).sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.9))
ax.barh(top_imp.index, top_imp.values, color=navy)
ax.set_xlabel("Drop in accuracy when shuffled (permutation importance)")
ax.grid(axis="x", linestyle="--", alpha=0.5)
plt.show()
```

Shuffle one predictor, measure the drop in accuracy. Importance says what the model **uses**, not what causes dropout.

---

## k-nearest neighbours

```python
tiny["distance"] = np.sqrt((tiny["stress"] - 3.5)**2 + (tiny["support"] - 3.0)**2)
tiny.sort_values("distance").head(3)
```

A new student with stress 3.5 and support 3.0.

The three nearest students vote: two considered dropping out, so $P(\text{Yes}) = 2/3$.

---

## The three nearest neighbours

```{python}
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3.9
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.9))

no_pts = tiny[tiny["dropout"] == "No"]
yes_pts = tiny[tiny["dropout"] == "Yes"]
ax.scatter(no_pts["stress"], no_pts["support"], color=navy, s=60, label="No")
ax.scatter(yes_pts["stress"], yes_pts["support"], color=copper, s=60, label="Yes")

ax.set_ylabel("Support")
ax.legend(title="Dropout", frameon=True)

```

Distances need predictors on one scale: the pipeline normalises them with `StandardScaler`.

---

## Tuning k

```python
knn_grid = GridSearchCV(
    Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("knn", KNeighborsClassifier())]),
    param_grid={"knn__n_neighbors": [1, 5, 11, 21, 41, 81]},
    cv=dropout_folds, scoring="roc_auc"
)
```

| k | 1 | 5 | 11 | 21 | 41 | 81 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| AUC | `{python} f2(knn_res[0])` | `{python} f2(knn_res[1])` | `{python} f2(knn_res[2])` | `{python} f2(knn_res[3])` | `{python} f2(knn_res[4])` | `{python} f2(knn_res[5])` |

The smoother k-NN becomes, the better: the pattern in this data is smooth.

---

## Support vector machines

- separate the classes with the widest empty "street", the **margin**;
- only the students closest to the boundary, the **support vectors**, place it;
- overlapping classes: some students may cross, at a cost ($C$);
- a **kernel** lets the boundary bend; the RBF kernel is popular.

```python
svm_linear = SVC(kernel="linear", probability=True, random_state=2026)
svm_rbf    = SVC(kernel="rbf", probability=True, random_state=2026)
```

---

## Four ways to draw a boundary

```{python}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 3.3
two_models = {
    "Logistic": Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()), ("clf", LogisticRegression())]),
    "Tree (depth 4)": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=10, random_state=2026),
    "k-NN (k = 21)": Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()), ("clf", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=21))]),
    "SVM (RBF)": Pipeline([("scaler", StandardScaler()), ("clf", SVC(kernel="rbf", probability=True, random_state=2026))])
}

X_tr_2 = X_train[["stress", "support"]]
s_vals = np.linspace(1, 5, 70)
sup_vals = np.linspace(1, 5, 70)
S, SUP = np.meshgrid(s_vals, sup_vals)
grid = pd.DataFrame({"stress": S.ravel(), "support": SUP.ravel()})
cmap = mcolors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("blue_orange", ["#eaf0f7", copper])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(10, 3.3), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, (title, model) in zip(axes, two_models.items()):
    model.fit(X_tr_2, y_train)
    prob = model.predict_proba(grid)[:, 1].reshape(S.shape)
    im = ax.pcolormesh(S, SUP, prob, cmap=cmap, vmin=0, vmax=1, shading="auto")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    ax.set_xlabel("Stress")

axes[0].set_ylabel("Support")
cbar = fig.colorbar(im, ax=axes.tolist(), shrink=0.7, label="P(Yes)")
plt.show()
```

Smooth gradient, rectangular blocks, patches, rounded regions. All agree: highest risk at high stress and low support.

---

## Comparing six models fairly

```python
candidate_models = {
    "logistic": Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("model", LogisticRegression())]),
    "svm_linear": Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("model", SVC(kernel="linear", probability=True))]),
    "forest": Pipeline([("prep", tree_recipe), ("model", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500))]),
    "svm_rbf": Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("model", SVC(kernel="rbf", probability=True))]),
    "knn": Pipeline([("prep", dropout_recipe), ("model", KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=41))]),
    "tree": Pipeline([("prep", tree_recipe), ("model", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4))]),
}

# Cross-validate each candidate pipeline on the identical 10 folds
```

Same folds for every model. Trees use the simple recipe, the others the normalised one.

---

## The simple model wins again

| Model | Cross-validated AUC | Std. error |
|---|---|---|
| logistic regression | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['logistic'][0])` | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['logistic'][1])` |
| random forest | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['forest'][0])` | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['forest'][1])` |
| linear SVM | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['svm_linear'][0])` | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['svm_linear'][1])` |
| k-NN (k = 41) | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['knn'][0])` | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['knn'][1])` |
| decision tree | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['tree'][0])` | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['tree'][1])` |
| RBF SVM | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['svm_rbf'][0])` | `{python} f2(ranked_dict['svm_rbf'][1])` |

Risk changes smoothly, with no thresholds for a tree to find. Logistic regression is kept, and explained in one sentence.

---

## From ranking to deciding

The AUC measures how well a model **ranks** students.

The counselling service needs a **decision**: contact this student or not.

A student is flagged when $P(\text{Yes})$ is above a **threshold**, 0.5 by default. The **confusion matrix** counts how the decisions turn out.

---

## The four outcomes

| | Truly at risk | Not at risk | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| **flagged** | 8 true positives | 4 false positives | 12 |
| **not flagged** | 2 false negatives | 86 true negatives | 88 |
| **total** | 10 | 90 | 100 |

A screening questionnaire given to 100 students, 10 truly at risk.

---

## Measures from the four counts

| Measure | Question | Here |
|---|---|---|
| sensitivity (recall) | how many at risk are found? | 8/10 = 80% |
| specificity | how many not at risk are left alone? | 86/90 = 96% |
| precision | how often is a contact justified? | 8/12 = 67% |
| F1 | precision and recall together | 0.73 |
| accuracy | share classified correctly | 94% |

---

## The study's model at 0.5

```python
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred_te, labels=[1, 0])
# [[8, 15], [3, 124]]
```

| Accuracy | Sensitivity | Specificity | Precision |
|---|---|---|---|
| `{python} pc(accuracy_score(y_test, y_pred_te))`% | `{python} pc(recall_score(y_test, y_pred_te))`% | 98% | `{python} pc(precision_score(y_test, y_pred_te))`% |

Of `{python} n_yes` at-risk test students, only `{python} tp50` are flagged. The model ranks well; the default 0.5 threshold is the problem.

---

## 0.5 is a default, not a law

| Lower threshold | Higher threshold |
|---|---|
| more students flagged | fewer students flagged |
| higher recall | higher precision |
| more false alarms | more students missed |

Here a flag means a conversation: cheap and harmless. Missing a student who leaves is costly. The threshold belongs well below 0.5.

---

## Choose the threshold without the test set

```python
cv_predictions = cross_val_predict(
    logistic_pipe, X_train, y_train, cv=dropout_folds, method="predict_proba"
)[:, 1]
```

Cross-validated predictions for every training student, each from a model that did not see them.

---

## The ROC curve

```{python}
#| fig-width: 5.5
#| fig-height: 4
fpr, tpr, thresholds = roc_curve(y_train, cv_predictions)
idx_05 = np.argmin(np.abs(thresholds - 0.5))
idx_02 = np.argmin(np.abs(thresholds - 0.2))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.5, 4))
ax.plot(fpr, tpr, color=navy, linewidth=2)
ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], linestyle="--", color="grey")
ax.scatter([fpr[idx_05], fpr[idx_02]], [tpr[idx_05], tpr[idx_02]], color=copper, s=50, zorder=5)
ax.annotate("t = 0.5", (fpr[idx_05], tpr[idx_05]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(10, -5), color=copper)
ax.annotate("t = 0.2", (fpr[idx_02], tpr[idx_02]), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(10, -5), color=copper)
ax.set_aspect("equal")
ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate")
ax.set_ylabel("Sensitivity")
plt.show()
```

Every threshold at once. The AUC is the area under the curve.

---

## The trade-off in a table

```{python}
#| results: asis
table_pct = threshold_table.copy()
for col in ["flagged", "recall", "precision", "specificity"]:
    table_pct[col] = (table_pct[col] * 100).round().astype(int).astype(str) + "%"
print(table_pct.to_markdown(index=False))
```

A lower threshold flags more students, finding more at risk at the cost of lower precision.

---

## Costs of the two errors

```python
cost_miss        = 10   # a student at risk who is not contacted
cost_false_alarm = 1    # an unnecessary conversation
```

Costs are judgements about consequences, not statistics. Make them explicit.

---

## The cheapest threshold

```{python}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.2
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.2))
ax.plot(cost_curve["threshold"], cost_curve["total_cost"], color=navy, linewidth=2)
ax.scatter(best_cost["threshold"], best_cost["total_cost"], color=copper, s=60, zorder=5)
ax.set_xlabel("Threshold")
ax.set_ylabel("Total cost")
plt.show()
```

Lowest at about `{python} best_cost['threshold']`, flagging `{python} pc(best_cost['flagged'])`% of students. Decision theory: $1 / (1 + 10) \approx 0.09$. Both say: far below 0.5.

---

## The threshold is a decision with an ethical side

- set costs with the people who will use the model;
- state them in the thesis;
- examine the effects on different groups;
- respect practical limits: counsellors cannot see everyone.

The counselling service settles on 0.2: flags about 26%, finds about 63% of those at risk, precision about 36%.

---

## Applying 0.2 to the test students

```python
flags_te = (y_prob_te >= 0.2).astype(int)
cm_02 = confusion_matrix(y_test, flags_te, labels=[1, 0])
# [[17, 6], [29, 98]]
```

The model now finds `{python} tp20` of `{python} n_yes` at-risk students instead of `{python} tp50`, flagging `{python} flag20` in all.

Accuracy fell to `{python} pc(accuracy_score(y_test, flags_te_02))`%. It does not matter: accuracy was never the goal.

---

## Report the threshold

Sensitivity, specificity, precision, and F1 all depend on the threshold.

Report which threshold was used, and why.

The AUC does not depend on it, which is why it is used to **compare** models.

---

## Imbalanced outcomes

| Remedy | How |
|---|---|
| move the threshold | flag at a lower probability |
| upsampling | repeat rare-class students |
| downsampling | drop common-class students |
| SMOTE | create artificial rare-class students |
| class weights | make rare-class mistakes count more |

Scikit-learn models support class weights directly via `class_weight='balanced'`.

---

## Class weighting / Upsampling

```python
balanced_pipe = Pipeline([
    ("prep", dropout_recipe),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", random_state=2026))
])
```

| | Sensitivity at 0.5 | AUC |
|---|---|---|
| balanced weighting | `{python} pc(up_sens)`% | `{python} f2(up_auc)` |

Weighting applies to training loss. It pushed probabilities up, like lowering the threshold, but did not improve ranking (AUC `{python} f2(up_auc)`).

After weighting, an output score of 0.6 no longer corresponds to a 60% empirical rate.

---

## Does the model work equally well for everyone?

| Test students at risk | Found at threshold 0.2 |
|---|---|
| women: 12 | 9 |
| men: 11 | 8 |

Similar shares, but too few students in the test set to detect subtle differences.

Check sensitivity and precision for every demographic group that matters, on as much data as possible.

## In your field: ecology

```python
penguins = dt.load_penguins().dropna(subset=["bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", "flipper_length_mm", "body_mass_g"])
p_rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=1)
p_rf.fit(p_X_train, p_y_train)
pd.crosstab(p_y_test, p_rf.predict(p_X_test))
```

Three penguin species from four morphological measurements: near 98% test accuracy.

Well-separated non-linear classes suit flexible tree ensembles.

## Troubleshooting guide (Part 1)

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| a tree changes completely between samples | trees are unstable; use a forest |
| k-NN dominated by one variable | predictors not normalised |
| best k at the edge of the grid | extend the grid |
| a flexible model loses | the pattern is smooth |

---

## Troubleshooting guide (Part 2)

| Symptom | Likely cause |
|---|---|
| high accuracy, few cases found | threshold too high for a rare outcome |
| threshold chosen on the test set | the test is spent; use cross-validation |
| sensitivity reported without a threshold | the number cannot be interpreted |
| probabilities too high after upsampling | resampling distorts probabilities |

---

## Completion checklist

- [ ] every model uses the same folds;
- [ ] preprocessing pipelines match each model's needs;
- [ ] models are compared by cross-validated AUC;
- [ ] the confusion matrix is read, not just accuracy;
- [ ] costs of both errors are stated;
- [ ] the threshold is chosen from cross-validated predictions;
- [ ] the threshold is reported;
- [ ] performance is checked for each subgroup.

---

## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 1)

| Misconception | Better mental model |
|---|---|
| flexible models always predict better | only when the pattern needs flexibility |
| importance shows cause | importance shows what the model uses |

---

## Misconceptions to leave behind (Part 2)

| Misconception | Better mental model |
|---|---|
| 0.5 is the right threshold | the threshold comes from costs |
| resampling improves a model | it usually shifts probabilities, not ranking |

---

## The chapter in one sentence

> **Compare models by how well they rank cases, then choose the threshold from what each kind of error costs, and report it.**
